job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Chloe Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Morning starts at my parents' flat in Leicester, where I sleep in what used to be my brother's room. I check the job boards over tea, send two or three applications, then walk to the library because home is too noisy. Afternoons I redo my CV or sit through video calls that go nowhere. I finished civil engineering eight months ago and the days feel long.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What did your degree and your short internship look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did civil engineering at De Montfort, with a placement of ten weeks at the regional water company, checking pipe survey drawings. My supervisor, Mrs Hargreave, liked my work but they weren't hiring graduates that year. My dad drives a city bus and he's a union rep, so he keeps asking who I've phoned. I have about six weeks of savings and some student debt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I finished civil engineering eight months ago and nobody near Leicester is hiring graduates. AI isn't what's stopping me, the economy is. I'd tell friends the hype was always louder than the product, and online I'd say nothing, since I don't use those tools anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it doesn't change my real problem, which is that nobody is hiring graduate civil engineers in my area. The water company froze its intake and two local firms laid people off last spring. So AI isn't the blocker, the jobs market is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, around 30 jobs a month, mostly to councils, the water company and the rail contractors. I'd ask Mrs Hargreave for a written reference and go to the engineering society's evening in March. If nothing comes by summer I'd take an agency job in a warehouse to cover my debt payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tired, mostly, and a bit ashamed when relatives ask. It feels steady but stuck, like waiting at a bus stop where the bus is late every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the economy is the problem, not AI. Who do you hold responsible for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I blame employers who cut graduate schemes to save money and then complain about a skills shortage. The government could fund public infrastructure jobs but keeps cutting them. I'd rather see my dad's union push for training places than watch companies decide alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would the agency job cost you, apart from the pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would cost me time to apply, because warehouse shifts start at six and I'd be wrecked by evening. It would also look bad on a CV for engineering roles, even though I'd need the money. My mum says a job is a job, but I worry it becomes a trap.

say: I'd tell people the **hype** was louder than the product and that careers like mine are still needed.
Online I'd stay quiet, because I don't use AI tools and don't want an argument.
think: Nobody is hiring graduate civil engineers near me, and that's a **jobs** problem, not an AI one.
I blame employers who cut graduate schemes and then complain about skills shortages.
do: Send about **30 applications** a month to councils, the water company and rail contractors.
Ask my internship supervisor for a **written reference** and attend the engineering society evening in March.
Take **agency warehouse work** by summer if no offer comes, to cover debt payments.
feel: Tired and a bit ashamed when relatives ask, like waiting for a **late bus**.
S0.quote: I finished civil engineering eight months ago and nobody near Leicester is hiring graduates. AI isn't what's stopping me, the economy is.
fieldNote: Her anxiety comes from her own **stalled search**, not from AI.
She sounds steady but has six weeks of savings and debt, which is why this isn't calm.
Blames employers and government, not technology, which fits her union family.

steps.text: Send 30 job applications a month to councils and contractors
Ask Mrs Hargreave for a written reference
Pay the minimum on student debt and track every bill

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the first thing in years that has me properly scared, and I'd say it publicly too. Coding, checking and planning are exactly the first jobs a graduate gets, and those are what the card says go first. I'd tell my dad's union they need a plan for young people now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the junior desk jobs I'd apply for, like checking survey data and drafting reports, get done by software first. Firms will hire fewer graduates and expect more from them. I'd be competing with people who already know the tools, and I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finally sit down and learn the basic software the firms use, probably the free course the engineering society offers, even though I dislike it. I'd target jobs on site with hands-on parts, like inspection and surveying, because robots come slower there. I'd also apply to the council, where my dad's friend Raj says they protect entry roles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried and a bit resentful. I don't want to be forced into tools I distrust, but I can see I may have no choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you distrust the tools. What exactly bothers you about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that nobody checks them. If a drawing is wrong, a bridge or a drain is wrong, and I don't see who takes the blame. I'd rather do the boring checking myself, but I know firms will pay less for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And if the council entry roles don't exist, what's your fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd try a master's in structural engineering, with my mum's help on fees. It buys me two years and a stronger CV, but it adds debt. I'd hate that, since I already feel I owe the bank.

say: I'd tell my dad's union they need a **plan for young people** now, before entry jobs vanish.
I'd tell friends this is the first change in years that really scares me.
think: Junior desk jobs like drafting reports and checking survey data go to software first.
Firms will hire **fewer graduates** and expect more, and I'd compete against people who already know the tools.
do: Take the engineering society's **free software course**, even though I dislike it.
Aim at **site inspection and surveying** jobs, where robots arrive later.
Apply to the council, where entry roles may be protected, and consider a **master's** as backup.
feel: Worried and resentful at being pushed toward tools I **distrust**.
S1.quote: If a drawing is wrong, a bridge or a drain is wrong, and I don't see who takes the blame.
fieldNote: Her distrust of AI is about **accountability** on safety-critical work, not fear of technology itself.
**Reluctant learner**: she plans the course but frames it as forced.
Shows the union upbringing: first instinct is a collective plan for young people.

steps.text: Take the engineering society's free software course
Apply for site inspection and surveying roles
Ask the council about protected entry roles through Raj
Push my dad's union branch to add youth training places

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster for people my age and the government has to act now. Two years is nothing. I'd write to my MP and join my dad at the union meeting, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree might lose its worth before I ever use it. If thinking work is done better and cheaper in two years, no firm hires a junior to check drawings. My one hope is that robots take about three more years, so site work lasts a little longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending and keep every pound I have, and I'd take any paid work to hold on to savings, even the warehouse. I'd ask the union about retraining grants and move my application hunt toward trades that need hands, like electrical fitting or site inspection. I'd also tell my parents I'm staying home longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. It feels like the floor is dropping while I'm still trying to find the stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, I'm sorry I took the degree, and he'd say don't be silly, it's not your fault. Then we'd both sit quiet in front of the news. He's seen his own job change twice already, so I think he'd stay calmer than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My phone contract and the little I spend on going out. Then I'd stop paying extra on my student loan and keep it as cash instead. My mum would hate that, since she thinks debt should be cleared first.

say: I'd say **two years is nothing** and the government must act now.
I'd write to my MP and go to my dad's **union meeting**, which I've never done.
think: My degree may lose its worth before I ever use it, since firms won't hire juniors to check drawings.
My one hope is that **robots** take about three more years, so site work lasts longer.
do: Stop extra loan payments and keep **every pound** as cash.
Take any paid work, even the warehouse, and ask the union about **retraining grants**.
Shift applications to trades that need hands, like **electrical fitting** and site inspection.
feel: Scared, like the floor is dropping while I look for the **stairs**.
S2.quote: My degree might lose its worth before I ever use it. If thinking work is done better and cheaper in two years, no firm hires a junior to check drawings.
fieldNote: Her **sense of time** shapes everything: with two years she moves from private worry to public action.
Alarmed because the entry jobs she wants are the first to vanish and she has little cushion.
The father is her emotional anchor; she expects him to cope better than she does.

steps.text: Stop extra loan payments and hold the cash
Take agency work to protect my savings
Go to a union meeting with my dad
Write to my MP about help for graduates

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to do something sensible, if the government and unions get moving. I'd want a public plan for retraining and for who owns the benefits. Otherwise a few firms keep all the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm calmer than with the two-year one, but still unsure my line of work survives. If I get a job in the next year, I'd have maybe three or four years of experience before the thinking work is automated. That's not enough to feel secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a job first, any engineering job, and use it to learn on site. Then I'd save hard for two years and pay off my loan quicker. I'd also join the union as soon as one exists at my employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mixed. Some hope because there's time, and some dread because I know how slowly governments move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you think the government would act in five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not unless people push, and that's why I'd get involved in the union. Raj's friends at the council said they've been told to plan for fewer entry roles already. So it feels like the plan is to wait and see.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what would you do differently if the job came in the first year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It sounds strange, but I'd want some life before everything changes. If a job comes in my first year, I'd finally move out and then save half of every pay cheque.

say: I'd say five years is enough to act if **unions and government** move together.
I'd ask for a public plan on retraining and on who owns the profits.
think: I'm calmer than with the two-year case, but a few years of experience may not be enough to be **secure**.
Governments move slowly, and the council is already planning for **fewer entry roles**.
do: Take **any engineering job** and use it to learn on site.
Save hard for two years and pay my **loan** down faster.
Join the **union** as soon as there's one at my employer.
feel: Hopeful because there's time, and dread because **governments** are slow.
S3.quote: I'd want some life before everything changes. If a job comes in my first year, I'd finally move out and then save half of every pay cheque.
fieldNote: With five years she plans in **sequence**: job first, then savings, then collective action.
Her trust is in organised workers more than in government promises.
Notable human detail: she wants a little life lived before the change arrives.

steps.text: Accept any engineering job and learn on site
Save half of every pay cheque
Join the union at my new employer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift if people use it well. A graduate like me could do a master's, learn a trade skill and still have time. I'd also say governments should start now with retraining funds.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel a lot more hopeful. In ten years I could be a senior site engineer, and the robots come about three years after the thinking AI, so there's still a bit of time. I'd hate to ignore it, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the first job, then study part time for a chartered engineer qualification, which firms respect. I'd save for a deposit, since property is something that doesn't disappear. I'd also help my dad's union write a youth training proposal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds long until I remember I've already spent eight months with no job. I feel calmer, but still guarded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the chartered qualification, in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it proves I can take legal responsibility for a design, and I can't see firms letting software sign off a bridge. It's slow and a bit boring, which suits me. My supervisor Mrs Hargreave got hers at 29 and says it changed everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want from the government in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid retraining that doesn't wipe out your savings, and public building projects that hire people. In my town, the new flood defences would give hundreds of jobs. That's the kind of thing I'd vote for.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** if governments start retraining funds now.
I'd tell friends to study and learn a trade skill while there's time.
think: I feel much more hopeful, since I could be a senior site engineer before the **robots** catch up.
Ten years sounds long, but I've already spent eight months without a job.
do: Take the first job and study part time for a **chartered engineer** qualification.
Save for a **deposit**, since property doesn't disappear.
Help my dad's union write a **youth training** proposal.
feel: Calmer but guarded, because ten years can **vanish** quickly.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds long until I remember I've already spent eight months with no job.
fieldNote: **Longest horizon** makes her most hopeful, but her recent job-search experience keeps her guarded.
Trusts credentials and slow professional routes, which fits her resistant style.
Policy ideas are concrete and local, like flood-defence building.

steps.text: Study part time for chartered engineer status
Help the union draft a youth training plan

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it leaves no time and my degree would be worthless before I use it. What would help is paid retraining, a union that fights for young people, and public building jobs. I'd also want a clear rule that people check what software designs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how it feels to be told to be flexible when you're twenty-three and already a bit stuck. People say just learn the tools. That only helps if someone is hiring at the end of it. My best hope is that employers rebuild graduate schemes, because nothing else works for people like me.

headlineQuote: People say just learn the tools. That only helps if someone is hiring at the end of it.
portrait: Chloe is a **civil engineering** graduate from Leicester, still without an offer eight months on.
She lives with her parents, and her dad, a bus driver and **union rep**, shapes how she sees work.
She avoids AI tools and trusts credentials, checking and public action more than new software.
Her mood moves with time: **alarmed** at two years, uneasy at ten.
She blames employers who cut graduate schemes, and wants unions and government to fund training and public building.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** AGI case, because her degree could lose its worth before she ever uses it.
whatWouldHelp: Paid retraining, a **union** that fights for young people, and public building jobs.
A clear rule that people check what software designs.
